title: Rethinking Fixed Temporal Grids: Frequency-Disentangled Motion Generation

paper.title: Rethinking Fixed Temporal Grids: Frequency-Disentangled Motion Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Most human motion generation methods encode motion as tokens on a uniform temporal grid, where every token spans the same fixed time window.
Human motion, however, is temporally heterogeneous: slowly evolving global trajectories coexist with rapid transient events such as foot contacts and joint impulses.
Forcing such multi-scale dynamics onto tokens of identical temporal resolution entangles motion frequencies, leaving slow regions redundant while smoothing out the rapid details that distinguish realistic motion.
We propose FreqMo , a scale-adaptive motion representation that decomposes motion into wavelet frequency bands, separating dynamics across temporal scales while preserving temporal localization and exact reconstruction.
Unified Frequency Residual Quantization (UFRQ) then encodes all bands within a single shared codebook, compressing the token sequence threefold and enabling stable single-stage generation.
Experiments show FreqMo attains SOTA fidelity with substantially improved high-frequency preservation, and the same decomposition transfers to continuous diffusion backbones.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Realistic human motion generation ( Khani et al. 2025 ; Xiao et al. 2025 ) underpins virtual reality ( Burdea and Coiffet 2003 ) , embodied intelligence ( Duan et al. 2022 ) , and digital human synthesis ( Varol et al. 2017 ) . Following language and vision ( Achiam et al. 2023 ; Peebles and Xie 2023 ) , prevailing methods encode motion on a fixed temporal grid where every token spans identical temporal support ( Cho et al. 2025 ; Dai et al. 2024 ; Lu et al. 2025 ) . This mirrors words in text or patches in images, where semantics reside within individual units and uniform discretization is well justified. Human motion, by contrast, is a continuous, non-stationary process whose semantics arise not from isolated poses but from temporally extended interactions: the evolution of a stride, the impulse of a landing, the deceleration into rest. Despite this distinction, few works question whether a fixed grid inherited from other modalities suits the dynamic nature of human motion (Figure 1 ). Figure 1: Left: Uniform grids induce temporal over-smoothing or redundancy. Right: FreqMo resolves it by adapting window sizes to intrinsic frequency scales. This oversight has concrete representational consequences. The inter-frame dynamics that define motion semantics are temporally heterogeneous, spanning orders of magnitude from slowly evolving global trajectories to near-instantaneous events such as foot contacts and joint impulses. A common practice augments each token with temporal derivatives (velocity, acceleration) ( Guo et al. 2022a ) , yet this captures higher-order statistics of the same entangled mixture rather than disentangling its frequency components. Since dynamics at distinct temporal scales correspond to distinct spectral frequencies, projecting them onto identically supported tokens forces these components to mix inseparably, leading to frequency entanglement (Figure 7 ) ( Yuan et al. 2024 ; Fu 2024 ) . Tokens spanning slow dynamics carry redundant information, while those spanning rapid transients smooth out the details they should preserve. This distortion originates at the representation level: a structural consequence of single-resolution indexing that no per-token enrichment can resolve, not a capacity deficit. Disentangling these frequencies is not as simple as transforming motion into the frequency domain. First, decomposing motion by frequency alone, as a global spectral transform does ( Fourier 1822 ) , records which frequencies occur but not when, untenable for motion, whose semantics are defined by precisely when events happen. A natural remedy reintroduces time through local windows ( Allen and Rabiner 1977 ) , but at a fixed scale: one window resolves all frequencies alike, too coarse for fast transients and too fine for slow trends. What motion needs is thus resolution that adapts to frequency, together with temporal localization. On this basis, we adopt the Wavelet Transform ( Mallat 1999 ) , whose variable-resolution filtering gives broad context to low-frequency trajectories and fine precision to high-frequency transients while preserving temporal resolution. This makes frequency disentanglement a property of the representation rather than the architecture. However, directly quantizing multi-scale wavelet features inevitably introduces quantization error. A residual scheme mitigates this, encoding each band against the reconstruction of the earlier ones. The order of this refinement, however, is decisive: the wavelet hierarchy runs from high-frequency detail to coarse global structure, so refining in that order would fix transient details before the low-frequency structure that anchors the motion. We instead encode coarse to fine, locking the global structure first so that residual error is confined to the high-frequency detail where it least matters. Building upon this, we present FreqMo , a scale-adaptive motion generation framework. FreqMo decomposes motion latents into hierarchical frequency bands via multi-level wavelet transform, aligning the representation with the intrinsic temporal scale of each dynamic component. To instantiate this in discrete generative models, we propose Unified Frequency Residual Quantization (UFRQ), which encodes all frequency bands into a single shared codebook through coarse-to-fine residual refinement, replacing fragmented multi-codebook pipelines and cutting the token sequence to one third of comparable designs. A scale-aware masked transformer ( Chang et al. 2022 ) then generates all bands simultaneously for stable single-stage generation. The decomposition is moreover agnostic to the generator: transplanting it into a continuous diffusion pipeline improves that model as well, showing the gain lies in the representation rather than any particular quantization scheme. The main contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify single-scale temporal rigidity as a structural limitation in existing motion representations and characterize the resulting frequency entanglement. • We propose Unified Frequency Residual Quantization, which encodes wavelet-disentangled bands into a single shared codebook while preserving temporal localization and exact reconstruction, replacing multi-stage residual pipelines with stable single-stage generation. • We show that the same representation improves generation quality under both discrete and continuous paradigms, confirming frequency disentanglement acts at the representation level and transfers across architectures.

sections.heading: Motion Latent Representation
sections.text: Learning an effective motion representation is a foundational challenge ( Liu et al. 2022 ; Siarohin et al. 2021 ; Zhu et al. 2023 ) . One major paradigm utilizes continuous latent spaces, typically via Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) ( Kingma and Welling 2013 ; Chen et al. 2023 ; Guo et al. 2022a ) , with recent methods operating directly on deterministic or causal latents ( Meng et al. 2025 ; Xiao et al. 2025 ; Yu et al. 2026 ) . However, the high precision of the continuous space can be detrimental, forcing the model to expend capacity encoding irrelevant, high-frequency noise and minor signal variations. This hinders generalization and complicates the subsequent generative task. An alternative paradigm learns a discrete representation using Vector Quantization (VQ-VAE) ( Van Den Oord et al. 2017 ) . By mapping poses to a finite codebook, VQ acts as a powerful regularizer, forcing the model to discard noise and learn a robust, semantic pose vocabulary ( Zhang et al. 2023a ; Jiang et al. 2023 ; Lu et al. 2025 ) . Given this robustness, our work builds upon the discrete quantization paradigm.

sections.heading: Motion Generative Models
sections.text: Given a latent representation, a generative model is required. Diffusion Models ( Ho et al. 2020 ; Meng et al. 2025 ; Weng et al. 2026 ) achieve strong quality by iteratively denoising a sequence, but suffer from computational overhead and slow inference. Autoregressive models ( Vaswani et al. 2017 ; Lu et al. 2025 ; Yu et al. 2026 ; Bian et al. 2025 ) generate tokens sequentially; while strong at capturing temporal dependencies, they are also slow and can accumulate errors. Multimodal and whole-body variants further extend this paradigm ( Xu et al. 2026 ; Zhang et al. 2026 ) . To balance these trade-offs, non-autoregressive masked transformers ( Chang et al. 2022 ; Pinyoanuntapong et al. 2024 ; Zeng et al. 2025 ) , inspired by BERT ( Devlin et al. 2019 ) , have emerged as a powerful alternative. By predicting masked tokens in parallel, these models enable fast inference while maintaining high quality via iterative refinement. Therefore, we build our generator upon the bidirectional masked transformer framework.

Given a text description 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , our goal is to generate a motion sequence 𝐗 = { 𝐱 t } t = 1 T \mathbf{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} , where each 𝐱 t ∈ ℝ J \mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{J} denotes the pose at frame t t . Conventional representations discretize motion on a uniform temporal grid, forcing dynamics at different temporal scales to share identical support and entangling them before generation begins. To resolve this, we introduce FreqMo , separating motion across temporal scales through two components: a frequency-disentangled representation that decomposes latent motion into multi-scale bands via wavelet transform and encodes them through UFRQ; and a text-conditioned masked transformer that generates all frequency tokens jointly while modeling their cross-scale dependencies. The wavelet decomposition is the core of FreqMo, and because it is independent of the generator, it applies to both continuous and discrete latent spaces.

sections.heading: Frequency-Disentangled Motion Representation
sections.text: A motion representation compresses raw motion into a compact, structured form that facilitates generation. Given a motion sequence 𝐗 ∈ ℝ T × J \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times J} , a motion encoder E M ​ ( ⋅ ) E_{M}(\cdot) projects it into continuous latent embeddings 𝐡 ∈ ℝ T ′ × d \mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T^{\prime}\times d} , where T ′ T^{\prime} is the downsampled temporal length and d d the embedding dimension. However, since E M E_{M} operates on a uniform temporal grid, 𝐡 \mathbf{h} conflates slowly evolving global trajectories and rapid local transients within the same fixed-resolution space. To resolve this, we decompose 𝐡 \mathbf{h} into a hierarchy of frequency-disentangled bands prior to any sequence modeling or quantization, ensuring that multi-scale dynamics are structurally separated at the representation level.

sections.heading: Wavelet-Based Frequency Decomposition.
sections.text: The decomposition operates through the discrete wavelet transform (DWT), applying a pair of complementary filters to separate frequency components. At decomposition level l l , given an input 𝐗 l ∈ ℝ T l × d \mathbf{X}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{l}\times d} with temporal length T l T_{l} , DWT produces: 𝐀 l , 𝐃 l = DWT ​ ( 𝐗 l ) , \mathbf{A}_{l},\mathbf{D}_{l}=\text{DWT}(\mathbf{X}_{l}), (1) where 𝐀 l ∈ ℝ T l + 1 × d \mathbf{A}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{l+1}\times d} is the approximation capturing smooth, low-frequency structure, and 𝐃 l ∈ ℝ T l + 1 × d \mathbf{D}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{l+1}\times d} the detail capturing rapid, high-frequency variations. Both are downsampled from T l T_{l} to T l + 1 < T l T_{l+1}<T_{l} . Starting from the initial latent embeddings 𝐗 1 = 𝐡 ∈ ℝ T ′ × d \mathbf{X}_{1}=\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T^{\prime}\times d} obtained from the motion encoder, DWT produces the first-level decomposition. However, the approximation 𝐀 1 \mathbf{A}_{1} still contains frequency variations that oscillate too slowly to be captured at the current temporal resolution. By recursively applying DWT to the approximation, setting 𝐗 l + 1 = 𝐀 l \mathbf{X}_{l+1}=\mathbf{A}_{l} , we progressively isolate slower frequency components at coarser temporal scales. This multi-scale hierarchy naturally emerges from the recursive decomposition, with temporal resolution decreasing as T 1 > T 2 > ⋯ > T L T_{1}>T_{2}>\cdots>T_{L} . This hierarchy is the frequency-disentangled representation: each band captures dynamics at a specific temporal scale, and exact invertibility ensures no kinematic information is discarded during decomposition.

sections.heading: Unified Frequency Residual Quantization
sections.text: Quantizing each band { 𝐀 L , 𝐃 l } \{\mathbf{A}_{L},\mathbf{D}_{l}\} independently would fragment the latent space across scales and let quantization errors at coarse levels irreversibly corrupt finer details. UFRQ avoids both by encoding bands from coarse to fine within a single shared codebook, progressively capturing reconstruction residuals. Starting from the coarsest band 𝐀 L \mathbf{A}_{L} (Algorithm 1 ), we iteratively quantize 𝐀 l \mathbf{A}_{l} , reconstruct a partial signal via IDWT (with high-frequency components zeroed), and compute the residual against the current signal. This residual is then decomposed to the next finer approximation 𝐀 l − 1 \mathbf{A}_{l-1} and quantized in the same way. All frequency bands share a single codebook 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , as wavelet decomposition naturally aligns coefficient magnitudes across levels. During decoding (Algorithm 2 ), quantized approximations are reconstructed in reverse order and accumulated, with the final residual added to recover the full signal. This coarse-to-fine encoding order ensures low-frequency structure is captured with high fidelity first, while quantization errors are relegated to less critical high-frequency bands through progressive residual refinement. sections.heading: Text-to-Motion Generation Model
sections.text: Given the pretrained representation, the task is to generate the token sequence 𝐳 = [ z L , … , z 1 , z 0 ] \mathbf{z}=[z_{L},\ldots,z_{1},z_{0}] conditioned on text 𝐜 \mathbf{c} (Figure 2 b). Unlike autoregressive or multi-stage methods, we use a bidirectional masked transformer ( Devlin et al. 2019 ) that produces all frequency bands simultaneously, reasoning globally across scales without cascaded pipelines. Text is encoded via CLIP ( Radford et al. 2021 ) , and a fraction ρ \rho of tokens in 𝐳 \mathbf{z} are replaced with [MASK] to obtain 𝐳 ~ \tilde{\mathbf{z}} . Each token carries a sinusoidal encoding of its normalized timestamp τ i = ( k + 0.5 ) / N l \tau_{i}=(k{+}0.5)/N_{l} ( k k indexing tokens within level l l ) and a learnable scale embedding 𝐬 l \mathbf{s}_{l} for its frequency level, aligning tokens from different resolutions that share the same physical time. A Transformer encoder then processes 𝐳 ~ \tilde{\mathbf{z}} via self-attention over the full sequence and cross-attention to text, predicting the original tokens at masked positions.

sections.heading: Inference
sections.text: At inference time (Figure 3 ), motion is generated from text in two stages. Given 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , the model first generates 𝐳 = [ z L , … , z 0 ] \mathbf{z}=[z_{L},\ldots,z_{0}] via iterative refinement: starting from all [MASK] tokens, it performs M M steps, at each step predicting confidence scores, unmasking the top k m k_{m} positions, and re-predicting remaining tokens. The completed sequence is decoded into 𝐡 ^ \hat{\mathbf{h}} via Algorithm 2 and passed to the motion decoder D M D_{M} to produce the final motion 𝐗 ^ \hat{\mathbf{X}} .

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: Datasets. We evaluate on two standard benchmarks: HumanML3D ( Guo et al. 2022a ) (14,616 motions, 44,970 texts) and KIT-ML ( Plappert et al. 2016 ) (3,911 motions, 6,278 descriptions), both mirrored for augmentation and split 0.8:0.05:0.15 into train/validation/test. Evaluation metrics. Following T2M ( Guo et al. 2022a ) , we report FID for motion quality, R-Precision (top-1/2/3) and Multimodal Distance for text-motion alignment, and Multimodality for diversity, prioritizing FID and R-Precision since diversity alone can reward degenerate solutions. To assess high-frequency preservation directly, we additionally report Acceleration Error and Jerk Error , the fidelity of second- and third-order motion derivatives. Implementation details. The encoder and decoder use residual blocks with downsampling factor 4. Wavelet decomposition uses L = 5 L=5 levels with db2 wavelets, and the shared codebook holds K = 512 K=512 codes of dimension d = 512 d=512 . The tokenizer is trained for 200k iterations (batch size 512, learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , commitment weight β = 0.25 \beta=0.25 ); the masked transformer has 8 layers, 6 heads, and hidden dimension 384, with masking ratio ρ = 0.3 \rho=0.3 . The generator is trained for 100k iterations (batch size 64) with the tokenizer frozen, and inference uses M = 12 M=12 refinement steps. All models are implemented in PyTorch on a single NVIDIA 4090 GPU.

sections.heading: Generation Performance
sections.text: Quantitative results. Table 1 compares FreqMo against state-of-the-art methods. FreqMo achieves the best FID on HumanML3D (0.040) and a competitive FID on KIT-ML (0.174). While ReMoDiffuse attains a lower FID (0.155) through retrieval augmentation, FreqMo operates without any external retrieval mechanism, making the comparison complementary rather than direct. For consistency, we compare only methods reporting averaged results with confidence intervals; single-run methods without variance (e.g., Light-T2M ( Zeng et al. 2025 ) ) are discussed in the appendix. Notably, evaluating the wavelet representation under a continuous paradigm (FreqMo-Diff), which replaces UFRQ with a VAE and diffusion decoder, consistently outperforms its frame-wise counterpart MLD ( Chen et al. 2023 ) , confirming the gains stem from the frequency-disentangled representation rather than the quantization scheme. Frequency structure: FreqMo vs. RQ-VAE. As the dominant multi-stage quantization baseline and the closest counterpart to UFRQ in token budget, RQ-VAE offers the natural comparison for internal latent organization. Figure 7 shows RQ-VAE exhibits entangled residuals with aliased spectra, each stage encoding an unstructured frequency mixture rather than isolating specific components. FreqMo instead produces cleanly separated bands, each capturing dynamics at a distinct temporal scale. This indicates UFRQ achieves genuine frequency disentanglement, not generic error reduction. Quality-efficiency trade-off. Figure 8 plots generation quality (FID) against inference speed (AIT, average inference time) on a log scale. FreqMo sits in the optimal bottom-left quadrant, being both faster and more accurate.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This work introduces FreqMo, which addresses an overlooked limitation in motion generation: frequency entanglement from uniform temporal tokenization. Decomposing motion into hierarchical frequency bands and encoding them in a unified codebook via coarse-to-fine residual quantization, FreqMo achieves SOTA fidelity with faithful high-frequency preservation. Its consistent gains across discrete and continuous paradigms confirm the improvement stems from the multi-scale representation, pointing to frequency-disentangled modeling as a direction beyond human motion.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.03012v1 [cs.CV] 02 Oct 2026 Rethinking Fixed Temporal Grids: Frequency-Disentangled Motion Generation Yunjiao Zhou Junlang Qian Gen Li Xinying Guo Lihua Xie Jianfei Yang Abstract Most human motion generation methods encode motion as tokens on a uniform temporal grid, where every token spans the same fixed time window. Human motion, however, is temporally heterogeneous: slowly evolving global trajectories coexist with rapid transient events such as foot contacts and joint impulses. Forcing such multi-scale dynamics onto tokens of identical temporal resolution entangles motion frequencies, leaving slow regions redundant while smoothing out the rapid details that distinguish realistic motion. We propose FreqMo , a scale-adaptive motion representation that decomposes motion into wavelet frequency bands, separating dynamics across temporal scales while preserving temporal localization and exact reconstruction. Unified Frequency Residual Quantization (UFRQ) then encodes all bands within a single shared codebook, compressing the token sequence threefold and enabling stable single-stage generation. Experiments show FreqMo attains SOTA fidelity with substantially improved high-frequency preservation, and the same decomposition transfers to continuous diffusion backbones. Nanyang Technological University, Singapore Introduction Realistic human motion generation ( Khani et al. 2025 ; Xiao et al. 2025 ) underpins virtual reality ( Burdea and Coiffet 2003 ) , embodied intelligence ( Duan et al. 2022 ) , and digital human synthesis ( Varol et al. 2017 ) . Following language and vision ( Achiam et al. 2023 ; Peebles and Xie 2023 ) , prevailing methods encode motion on a fixed temporal grid where every token spans identical temporal support ( Cho et al. 2025 ; Dai et al. 2024 ; Lu et al. 2025 ) . This mirrors words in text or patches in images, where semantics reside within individual units and uniform discretization is well justified. Human motion, by contrast, is a continuous, non-stationary process whose semantics arise not from isolated poses but from temporally extended interactions: the evolution of a stride, the impulse of a landing, the deceleration into rest. Despite this distinction, few works question whether a fixed grid inherited from other modalities suits the dynamic nature of human motion (Figure 1 ). Figure 1: Left: Uniform grids induce temporal over-smoothing or redundancy. Right: FreqMo resolves it by adapting window sizes to intrinsic frequency scales. This oversight has concrete representational consequences. The inter-frame dynamics that define motion semantics are temporally heterogeneous, spanning orders of magnitude from slowly evolving global trajectories to near-instantaneous events such as foot contacts and joint impulses. A common practice augments each token with temporal derivatives (velocity, acceleration) ( Guo et al. 2022a ) , yet this captures higher-order statistics of the same entangled mixture rather than disentangling its frequency components. Since dynamics at distinct temporal scales correspond to distinct spectral frequencies, projecting them onto identically supported tokens forces these components to mix inseparably, leading to frequency entanglement (Figure 7 ) ( Yuan et al. 2024 ; Fu 2024 ) . Tokens spanning slow dynamics carry redundant information, while those spanning rapid transients smooth out the details they should preserve. This distortion originates at the representation level: a structural consequence of single-resolution indexing that no per-token enrichment can resolve, not a capacity deficit. Disentangling these frequencies is not as simple as transforming motion into the frequency domain. First, decomposing motion by frequency alone, as a global spectral transform does ( Fourier 1822 ) , records which frequencies occur but not when, untenable for motion, whose semantics are defined by precisely when events happen. A natural remedy reintroduces time through local windows ( Allen and Rabiner 1977 ) , but at a fixed scale: one window resolves all frequencies alike, too coarse for fast transients and too fine for slow trends. What motion needs is thus resolution that adapts to frequency, together with temporal localization. On this basis, we adopt the Wavelet Transform ( Mallat 1999 ) , whose variable-resolution filtering gives broad context to low-frequency trajectories and fine precision to high-frequency transients while preserving temporal resolution. This makes frequency disentanglement a property of the representation rather than the architecture. However, directly quantizing multi-scale wavelet features inevitably introduces quantization error. A residual scheme mitigates this, encoding each band against the reconstruction of the earlier ones. The order of this refinement, however, is decisive: the wavelet hierarchy runs from high-frequency detail to coarse global structure, so refining in that order would fix transient details before the low-frequency structure that anchors the motion. We instead encode coarse to fine, locking the global structure first so that residual error is confined to the high-frequency detail where it least matters. Building upon this, we present FreqMo , a scale-adaptive motion generation framework. FreqMo decomposes motion latents into hierarchical frequency bands via multi-level wavelet transform, aligning the representation with the intrinsic temporal scale of each dynamic component. To instantiate this in discrete generative models, we propose Unified Frequency Residual Quantization (UFRQ), which encodes all frequency bands into a single shared codebook through coarse-to-fine residual refinement, replacing fragmented multi-codebook pipelines and cutting the token sequence to one third of comparable designs. A scale-aware masked transformer ( Chang et al. 2022 ) then generates all bands simultaneously for stable single-stage generation. The decomposition is moreover agnostic to the generator: transplanting it into a continuous diffusion pipeline improves that model as well, showing the gain lies in the representation rather than any particular quantization scheme. The main contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify single-scale temporal rigidity as a structural limitation in existing motion representations and characterize the resulting frequency entanglement. • We propose Unified Frequency Residual Quantization, which encodes wavelet-disentangled bands into a single shared codebook while preserving temporal localization and exact reconstruction, replacing multi-stage residual pipelines with stable single-stage generation. • We show that the same representation improves generation quality under both discrete and continuous paradigms, confirming frequency disentanglement acts at the representation level and transfers across architectures. Related Work Motion Latent Representation Learning an effective motion representation is a foundational challenge ( Liu et al. 2022 ; Siarohin et al. 2021 ; Zhu et al. 2023 ) . One major paradigm utilizes continuous latent spaces, typically via Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) ( Kingma and Welling 2013 ; Chen et al. 2023 ; Guo et al. 2022a ) , with recent methods operating directly on deterministic or causal latents ( Meng et al. 2025 ; Xiao et al. 2025 ; Yu et al. 2026 ) . However, the high precision of the continuous space can be detrimental, forcing the model to expend capacity encoding irrelevant, high-frequency noise and minor signal variations. This hinders generalization and complicates the subsequent generative task. An alternative paradigm learns a discrete representation using Vector Quantization (VQ-VAE) ( Van Den Oord et al. 2017 ) . By mapping poses to a finite codebook, VQ acts as a powerful regularizer, forcing the model to discard noise and learn a robust, semantic pose vocabulary ( Zhang et al. 2023a ; Jiang et al. 2023 ; Lu et al. 2025 ) . Given this robustness, our work builds upon the discrete quantization paradigm. Motion Generative Models Given a latent representation, a generative model is required. Diffusion Models ( Ho et al. 2020 ; Meng et al. 2025 ; Weng et al. 2026 ) achieve strong quality by iteratively denoising a sequence, but suffer from computational overhead and slow inference. Autoregressive models ( Vaswani et al. 2017 ; Lu et al. 2025 ; Yu et al. 2026 ; Bian et al. 2025 ) generate tokens sequentially; while strong at capturing temporal dependencies, they are also slow and can accumulate errors. Multimodal and whole-body variants further extend this paradigm ( Xu et al. 2026 ; Zhang et al. 2026 ) . To balance these trade-offs, non-autoregressive masked transformers ( Chang et al. 2022 ; Pinyoanuntapong et al. 2024 ; Zeng et al. 2025 ) , inspired by BERT ( Devlin et al. 2019 ) , have emerged as a powerful alternative. By predicting masked tokens in parallel, these models enable fast inference while maintaining high quality via iterative refinement. Therefore, we build our generator upon the bidirectional masked transformer framework. Method Figure 2: Model structure for FreqMo during training. Given a text description 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , our goal is to generate a motion sequence 𝐗 = { 𝐱 t } t = 1 T \mathbf{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} , where each 𝐱 t ∈ ℝ J \mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{J} denotes the pose at frame t t . Conventional representations discretize motion on a uniform temporal grid, forcing dynamics at different temporal scales to share identical support and entangling them before generation begins. To resolve this, we introduce FreqMo , separating motion across temporal scales through two components: a frequency-disentangled representation that decomposes latent motion into multi-scale bands via wavelet transform and encodes them through UFRQ; and a text-conditioned masked transformer that generates all frequency tokens jointly while modeling their cross-scale dependencies. The wavelet decomposition is the core of FreqMo, and because it is independent of the generator, it applies to both continuous and discrete latent spaces. Frequency-Disentangled Motion Representation A motion representation compresses raw motion into a compact, structured form that facilitates generation. Given a motion sequence 𝐗 ∈ ℝ T × J \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times J} , a motion encoder E M ​ ( ⋅ ) E_{M}(\cdot) projects it into continuous latent embeddings 𝐡 ∈ ℝ T ′ × d \mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T^{\prime}\times d} , where T ′ T^{\prime} is the downsampled temporal length and d d the embedding dimension. However, since E M E_{M} operates on a uniform temporal grid, 𝐡 \mathbf{h} conflates slowly evolving global trajectories and rapid local transients within the same fixed-resolution space. To resolve this, we decompose 𝐡 \mathbf{h} into a hierarchy of frequency-disentangled bands prior to any sequence modeling or quantization, ensuring that multi-scale dynamics are structurally separated at the representation level. Wavelet-Based Frequency Decomposition. The decomposition operates through the discrete wavelet transform (DWT), applying a pair of complementary filters to separate frequency components. At decomposition level l l , given an input 𝐗 l ∈ ℝ T l × d \mathbf{X}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{l}\times d} with temporal length T l T_{l} , DWT produces: 𝐀 l , 𝐃 l = DWT ​ ( 𝐗 l ) , \mathbf{A}_{l},\mathbf{D}_{l}=\text{DWT}(\mathbf{X}_{l}), (1) where 𝐀 l ∈ ℝ T l + 1 × d \mathbf{A}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{l+1}\times d} is the approximation capturing smooth, low-frequency structure, and 𝐃 l ∈ ℝ T l + 1 × d \mathbf{D}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{l+1}\times d} the detail capturing rapid, high-frequency variations. Both are downsampled from T l T_{l} to T l + 1 < T l T_{l+1}<T_{l} . Starting from the initial latent embeddings 𝐗 1 = 𝐡 ∈ ℝ T ′ × d \mathbf{X}_{1}=\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T^{\prime}\times d} obtained from the motion encoder, DWT produces the first-level decomposition. However, the approximation 𝐀 1 \mathbf{A}_{1} still contains frequency variations that oscillate too slowly to be captured at the current temporal resolution. By recursively applying DWT to the approximation, setting 𝐗 l + 1 = 𝐀 l \mathbf{X}_{l+1}=\mathbf{A}_{l} , we progressively isolate slower frequency components at coarser temporal scales. After L L levels, this yields a hierarchy of frequency bands: 𝐀 L ∈ ℝ T L × d , { 𝐃 l ∈ ℝ T l + 1 × d } l = 1 L , \mathbf{A}_{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{L}\times d},\quad\{\mathbf{D}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{l+1}\times d}\}_{l=1}^{L}, (2) where lower-indexed bands ( 𝐃 1 \mathbf{D}_{1} ) encode finer, higher-frequency dynamics at higher temporal resolution and higher-indexed bands ( 𝐃 L \mathbf{D}_{L} ) encode coarser, lower-frequency changes at lower resolution. This multi-scale hierarchy naturally emerges from the recursive decomposition, with temporal resolution decreasing as T 1 > T 2 > ⋯ > T L T_{1}>T_{2}>\cdots>T_{L} . Crucially, the wavelet transform guarantees perfect reconstruction via inverse DWT (IDWT): 𝐗 l = IDWT ​ ( 𝐀 l , 𝐃 l ) , \mathbf{X}_{l}=\text{IDWT}(\mathbf{A}_{l},\mathbf{D}_{l}), (3) so that 𝐡 ^ = IDWT L ​ ( 𝐀 L , { 𝐃 l } l = 1 L ) \hat{\mathbf{h}}=\text{IDWT}^{L}(\mathbf{A}_{L},\{\mathbf{D}_{l}\}_{l=1}^{L}) recovers the original representation losslessly. This hierarchy is the frequency-disentangled representation: each band captures dynamics at a specific temporal scale, and exact invertibility ensures no kinematic information is discarded during decomposition. Unified Frequency Residual Quantization Quantizing each band { 𝐀 L , 𝐃 l } \{\mathbf{A}_{L},\mathbf{D}_{l}\} independently would fragment the latent space across scales and let quantization errors at coarse levels irreversibly corrupt finer details. UFRQ avoids both by encoding bands from coarse to fine within a single shared codebook, progressively capturing reconstruction residuals. Starting from the coarsest band 𝐀 L \mathbf{A}_{L} (Algorithm 1 ), we iteratively quantize 𝐀 l \mathbf{A}_{l} , reconstruct a partial signal via IDWT (with high-frequency components zeroed), and compute the residual against the current signal. This residual is then decomposed to the next finer approximation 𝐀 l − 1 \mathbf{A}_{l-1} and quantized in the same way. All frequency bands share a single codebook 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , as wavelet decomposition naturally aligns coefficient magnitudes across levels. During decoding (Algorithm 2 ), quantized approximations are reconstructed in reverse order and accumulated, with the final residual added to recover the full signal. This coarse-to-fine encoding order ensures low-frequency structure is captured with high fidelity first, while quantization errors are relegated to less critical high-frequency bands through progressive residual refinement. Bold: best result, underline: second best. Setup Datasets. We evaluate on two standard benchmarks: HumanML3D ( Guo et al. 2022a ) (14,616 motions, 44,970 texts) and KIT-ML ( Plappert et al. 2016 ) (3,911 motions, 6,278 descriptions), both mirrored for augmentation and split 0.8:0.05:0.15 into train/validation/test. Evaluation metrics. Following T2M ( Guo et al. 2022a ) , we report FID for motion quality, R-Precision (top-1/2/3) and Multimodal Distance for text-motion alignment, and Multimodality for diversity, prioritizing FID and R-Precision since diversity alone can reward degenerate solutions. To assess high-frequency preservation directly, we additionally report Acceleration Error and Jerk Error , the fidelity of second- and third-order motion derivatives. Implementation details. The encoder and decoder use residual blocks with downsampling factor 4. Wavelet decomposition uses L = 5 L=5 levels with db2 wavelets, and the shared codebook holds K = 512 K=512 codes of dimension d = 512 d=512 . The tokenizer is trained for 200k iterations (batch size 512, learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , commitment weight β = 0.25 \beta=0.25 ); the masked transformer has 8 layers, 6 heads, and hidden dimension 384, with masking ratio ρ = 0.3 \rho=0.3 . The generator is trained for 100k iterations (batch size 64) with the tokenizer frozen, and inference uses M = 12 M=12 refinement steps. All models are implemented in PyTorch on a single NVIDIA 4090 GPU. Generation Performance Quantitative results. Table 1 compares FreqMo against state-of-the-art methods. FreqMo achieves the best FID on HumanML3D (0.040) and a competitive FID on KIT-ML (0.174). While ReMoDiffuse attains a lower FID (0.155) through retrieval augmentation, FreqMo operates without any external retrieval mechanism, making the comparison complementary rather than direct. For consistency, we compare only methods reporting averaged results with confidence intervals; single-run methods without variance (e.g., Light-T2M ( Zeng et al. 2025 ) ) are discussed in the appendix. Notably, evaluating the wavelet representation under a continuous paradigm (FreqMo-Diff), which replaces UFRQ with a VAE and diffusion decoder, consistently outperforms its frame-wise counterpart MLD ( Chen et al. 2023 ) , confirming the gains stem from the frequency-disentangled representation rather than the quantization scheme. Frequency structure: FreqMo vs. RQ-VAE. As the dominant multi-stage quantization baseline and the closest counterpart to UFRQ in token budget, RQ-VAE offers the natural comparison for internal latent organization. Figure 7 shows RQ-VAE exhibits entangled residuals with aliased spectra, each stage encoding an unstructured frequency mixture rather than isolating specific components. FreqMo instead produces cleanly separated bands, each capturing dynamics at a distinct temporal scale. This indicates UFRQ achieves genuine frequency disentanglement, not generic error reduction. Conclusion This work introduces FreqMo, which addresses an overlooked limitation in motion generation: frequency entanglement from uniform temporal tokenization. Decomposing motion into hierarchical frequency bands and encoding them in a unified codebook via coarse-to-fine residual quantization, FreqMo achieves SOTA fidelity with faithful high-frequency preservation. Its consistent gains across discrete and continuous paradigms confirm the improvement stems from the multi-scale representation, pointing to frequency-disentangled modeling as a direction beyond human motion.
